_doc: ⚑ S209 / P7-47 — THE LEXICON (his, 2026-10-02: "'The Lexicon — Multimedia Edition' — love this! I like your design proposal"; "the word of the day could be quite good"). Generated from docs/reinterp/RESEARCH_LEXICON_2026-10-02.md (every claim sourced there; statuses read by hand from its Evidence lines — the word's USE is documented for all of them; `status` is what its CLAIM is). The 'line' is the seller's Word of the Day (operable: it mocks only the programme's pitch, never the people); the 'close' is the Lexicon's own plain sentence. No Word of the Day for SOGICE, detransition or chosen family (the research's ethics notes). Shown at the Close on Daniel's machine (src/room/lexicon.ts) and, one word per era, as each update's own 'word of the day' app.
title: THE LEXICON
sub: the words they used, and the reasons they gave · 1997–2026

statusLabels.moral: A moral frame, not a finding
statusLabels.political: A political frame, not a finding
statusLabels.half: Half right, and the half that matters is wrong

reasonsIntro: What the networks said caused people to be gay, lesbian, bisexual or trans. The reasons change with the decades; their shape does not: the cause is placed in a family injury or a deficit, so the person becomes the symptom.
arc: 1997 — father, mother, abuse, unmet needs, choice. Said with confidence.
2003 — the same, with testimonies as proof.
2016 — for lesbian women: the mother wound, emotional dependency, abuse, a ‘spiritual fallacy’.
2026 — for trans people: confusion, trauma, ‘gender ideology’, and peer influence or ‘social contagion’, with the ‘signs’ parents reported in a 2018 survey. The method offered: exploring first.
yoursNone: You met none of them by name. They were there anyway.
yoursIntro: The words that reached you, in the order they did:
sources: More sources: open the menu, then Credits & attributions.
sourcesIntro: The research behind these words and reasons.

terms.close: A phrase ministries prefer to “gay” or “lesbian”. It frames attraction as a feeling to be reduced, not part of who someone is. Mainstream health bodies reject that framing.
terms.line: Just a feeling you have, like a cold. Not who you are. Feeling lighter already?

terms.close: “Unwanted” suggests a free choice. Research finds the wish to change usually comes from religious or family pressure, and many people exposed to change efforts were minors.
terms.line: Nobody made you want this to stop. You just… noticed that everyone around you does.
terms.soundTitle: The Family Form's music box (1997, this piece's own)

terms.close: A word that casts being gay as a battle to be fought. The people who use it describe their own desires as a temptation; major health bodies do not.
terms.line: Struggling means you're trying. Good for you! (We'll tell you what you're trying to do.)
terms.soundTitle: “Fold My Hands”, the prayer tape (1997, this piece's own)

terms.close: What ministries call a gay person who resists their own desire. It makes the fight the person’s name, so the fight never ends. Members of these groups used it of themselves; the research records the word, it does not endorse it.
terms.line: You fight it. That makes you one of us!

terms.close: A word that treats being gay as a habit or a choice. Attraction is not chosen, and health bodies describe it as a normal variation of human sexuality.
terms.line: Like a gym membership, but with a view on eternity. You can cancel any time!

terms.close: “Ex-gay” claims that orientation can be left behind. Research finds change efforts rarely change attraction and often harm. Many people who tried now call themselves ex-ex-gay.
terms.line: Everything you were before today is former. Isn't that nice? Say it again, softly.
terms.soundTitle: “Discover the New You”, the broadcast jingle (1997, this piece's own)

terms.close: A word that treats attraction as an enemy. The “overcome, don't eliminate” version is a retreat from earlier promises of change, not a finding that it works.
terms.line: Today you overcame a thought. Tomorrow: another thought! Overcoming never stops. Neither do we.
terms.soundTitle: Restorify Media's testimony bed (2003, this piece's own)

terms.close: A word that treats sexuality as damage. No orientation is a disorder; the damage described in research comes from stigma and from change efforts themselves.
terms.line: Good news! If you're broken, you're fixable. (Terms and conditions apply to the fixing.)

terms.close: The idea that being gay is a symptom of a hidden hurt. Researchers reviewing the evidence found no such root; theories blaming family patterns have been discredited.
terms.line: Every flower has one. Let's dig yours up and look at it together. Don't worry; it'll hurt a little.

terms.close: The claim that a distant father or smothering mother makes a child gay. Studies do not support it; a painful childhood is real for some, but does not decide orientation.
terms.line: It's not your fault. It's your father's. (Or your mother's. We'll find out together.)
terms.soundTitle: Release Work's tape (1997, this piece's own)

terms.close: A term for treating lesbian love as a disorder of “needing too much”. Researchers who studied the movement describe it as a euphemism, not a clinical finding.
terms.line: Loving someone too much is a symptom. Don't worry, we have a worksheet for love.
terms.soundTitle: GracePlatform's calm loop (2016, this piece's own)

terms.close: “Gender confusion” is not a medical term. Current diagnostic manuals use “gender dysphoria” or “gender incongruence”. The word has been used to read ordinary gender nonconformity as a problem.
terms.line: Feeling confused? Wonderful. That means we can start by clarifying you.

terms.close: A trademarked name for therapy aimed at reducing same-sex attraction. Mainstream associations oppose it; studies find it does not work and can harm.
terms.line: Tiny repairs, every week. Like a hotel, but for your insides.

terms.close: A newer name for therapy linked to reparative therapy. Its providers deny it aims to change orientation; researchers and forensic experts classify it with change efforts.
terms.line: Same cure, bigger word. Please don't call it a cure.

terms.close: Short for efforts to change or suppress sexual orientation, gender identity or expression. Used by researchers and survivors; practitioners usually call it something gentler.
An umbrella term for efforts to change or suppress who someone is. Major health bodies reject it. It is banned in a growing number of places and rebrands when banned.
terms.line: We don't do the other thing. We just talk. About changing.

terms.close: A peer asked to monitor and report someone's behaviour. Support in itself is not harmful; here it was used to police a person's identity and treat lapses as failure.
terms.line: Someone who loves you will always want to know where you were.
terms.soundTitle: The Fellowship Network's page music (1997, this piece's own)

terms.close: Words that present being gay as a captivity or injury. The research on these programmes finds the “freedom” was rarely delivered, and the harm that followed was real.
terms.line: The door is open. (Please use the door we pointed at.)
terms.soundTitle: “Chase the Clouds”, Restorify's jingle (2003, this piece's own)
terms.later: In this piece's 2026 the word moves into software: a session, a profile “restored”. That use is invented; no real tool that “restores” a person's photo was found.

terms.close: “Affirming” has two meanings. Therapists use it for acceptance without a set outcome. Change programmes used it for affirming “masculinity” or “femininity” as defined by them.
terms.line: We affirm everything about you! (Except the part you came in with.)

terms.close: A label used since the 2010s for gender studies, trans rights and sex education as one hidden agenda. Researchers describe it as a political frame, not a scientific claim.
terms.line: Everyone else has one. We just have the truth.

terms.close: The claim that gender identity spreads among friends or online. It began as parents' reports; no validated clinical entity exists. Reviews call the topic contested and caution against simple explanations.
terms.line: Protect yours! (We've already tidied it for you.)
terms.soundTitle: THE GREAT BECOMING, the AI's video of her week (2026, invented): “18 today. And it had spread.”
terms.later: In this piece's 2026 the frame is said to one person: “it spread to you”, ticked off the 2018 paper's parent-reported “signs”. The AI, and its use of them as a checklist, are this piece's invention.

terms.close: A label from a 2018 survey that asked only parents. They reported the “signs”: a sudden announcement, friends coming out too, more time online. Its 2019 correction says it is “not a formal mental health diagnosis”.
terms.sold: “I checked your week against the signs. They're all there.”
terms.soldFrom: Second Thoughts, the AI in this piece (invented; it never names the label)
terms.soundTitle: THE GREAT BECOMING, the AI's video of her week (2026, invented): “Suddenly. Just like her friends.”

terms.close: “Desistance” means a child's gender-variant feelings fading. Studies from the 1980s onward are disputed over how they counted children and what the numbers mean for care today.
terms.line: Children grow out of things. You did. We saw you grow.

terms.close: Some people stop or reverse a gender transition, for many reasons, including regret, stigma, family pressure and changed understanding. Both their care and the way campaigns use their stories matter.
“Exploratory” therapy says it only helps people think. Supporters deny it is conversion therapy; critics say it steers people away from transition. The question is disputed.
terms.line: No pressure. No conclusions. Only a gentle, endless not yet.
terms.later: In 2025–26 the word reached policy. A US report put “exploratory therapy” first; critics say it can include conversion practices. The draft ban for England and Wales says it does not ban “explorative conversations”.

terms.close: A US government report (May 2025) puts talk therapy first, “exploratory therapy” among it, and calls equating it with conversion therapy “misguided”. The American Academy of Pediatrics and others say it can include conversion practices.

The UK government's draft ban on conversion practices in England and Wales (June 2026) covers sexual orientation and gender identity. It says it does not ban “explorative conversations”. A joint committee is scrutinising it.
terms.sold: “And here, the new bill says it won't ban ‘explorative conversations’.”
terms.soldFrom: Second Thoughts, the AI in this piece (invented)

terms.close: Words of eligibility. A UK helpline for young people says it is run “for and by same-sex attracted people”. After a 2025 court ruling on “biological sex”, some groups closed membership to trans women. Others chose to stay open.
terms.sold: “Even the LGB group says you're not one of them.”
terms.soldFrom: THE GREAT BECOMING, the AI's video (invented): the refusal turned against her
terms.soundTitle: THE GREAT BECOMING, the AI's video of her week (2026, invented)

terms.close: Family made by choice and care, not blood. For people rejected by their families, it can be a source of safety and support.
terms.soundTitle: transjesus.str, the people's music (2026, this piece's own)

terms.close: Scientists do not know exactly why orientation varies, and no single cause has been found. That does not show it can be changed; research finds attempts do not work. A church agency trained its counsellors (module captured 2005) to call ‘born that way’ a lie.
terms.line: Nobody's found one! (That settles everything. Don't read the rest.)

terms.close: The idea that same-sex attraction is really an unmet need for love in disguise. It is a theory from the 1980s; researchers have not found it to be true.
terms.line: You have needs! Wonderful. We'll tell you which ones are legitimate.

terms.close: A church agency's counsellor module (captured 2005) called being gay an ‘orientation problem’ and graded people by ‘symptoms’ — mild, moderate, severe — counting how often they had loved men. Being gay is not an illness.
terms.line: Mild, moderate or severe? Take our two-minute quiz! (There is no fourth option.)

men.reason: A distant, absent or rejecting father (“father hunger”)
Peer rejection, being “not man enough”, childhood gender nonconformity (“gender esteem”; “prehomosexual boy”; “chronic juvenile unmasculinity”)
Sexual abuse or “premature exposure to sexual experience”
men.status: NOT SUPPORTED as a cause of orientation

men.reason: Fear of heterosexual men (“heterophobia”), offered to rebut “internalised homophobia”
A series of decisions / habit / sin (“agency”)
men.status: NOT AN EMPIRICAL CLAIM for the moral half

men.reason: Pornography, masturbation, fantasy as a trap
men.status: no source gives it as a cause

men.reason: “Biology, environment and early development all play a role” (the softened version)
Trauma and “attachment loss” in a clinical dress (“symbolic defense against attachment loss”; “signal”)
men.status: NOT SUPPORTED as a cause of orientation

men.reason: Four stages — ‘confusion’, ‘filling the void’, ‘sexual identity crisis’, ‘resolution’ — and being born this way denied as doctrine
The programme's own members, asked in 2004, named the programme's causes: father 97%, male peers 97%, mother 91%; 95% rejected ‘born this way’

women.reason: The mother wound: failed attachment to the mother, “disidentification” with her femininity
Sexual abuse as a path from femininity
A passive or unavailable father who fails to protect; or a father who does not affirm her
Peer labelling and “friends who affirm femininity” lacking
Fear of, or inability to relate to, men / the opposite sex
Feminism, women's colleges, “older lesbians” as influence
Lesbianism as “an identity crisis, not a sexual orientation problem”
“Spiritual fallacy”: a cold, distant, uncaring picture of God learned at home or church

trans.reason: “Gender confusion” / disturbed gender development from family dynamics (parents tolerating cross-gender behaviour “as a phase”; maternal difficulties; distant fathers)
Trauma, abuse, mental-health conditions, maladaptive coping
trans.status: CONTESTED: some individuals' own reading, not an established cause. Cass notes gender distress can manifest “like eating disorders or depression” in some, as one of several possibilities

trans.reason: Parent-child conflict as an alternative explanation
Homophobia or difficulty accepting being lesbian, gay or bi as a driver of trans identity
Availability of puberty blockers as an explanation for rising referrals
The “signs”: a sudden announcement, friends coming out too, more time online, more popular after, earlier mental-health conditions (parents' reports)
trans.status: CONTESTED: parents' reports only; “not a formal mental health diagnosis” (2019 correction)
